Hon'ble Mrs. Sunita Agarwal,J.

Heard Sri Santosh Kumar Srivastava, holding brief of Sri Brij Raj Singh, learned Advocate for the
revisionist and learned Aga for the State-respondent.

The present revisionist is directed against the judgement and order dated 30.07.1997 passed by the Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate, Mainpuri in Case No. 645 of 1994 under Sections 7/16 of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.
It appears that a complaint was lodged on 28.09.1988 after receipt of public analyst report regarding sample of milk taken from the possession of the revisionist by the Food Inspector on 29.12.1987.
From the perusal of the order impugned, it transpires that sample was sent to the public analyst on 2.01.1988 and report was received on 02.02.1988.

After receipt of public analyst report, the Food Tejpal Singh vs State Of U.P. on 21 November, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/13960054/

sentences.text: In the meantime, the Food Inspector, namely Sri R.N. Saxena who had taken the sample had died.

Before the Court below, a witness of the sample taken by the then Food Inspector, namely Sri R.N. Saxena had been produced as P.W.-3 to prove that sample was taken after proper shaking of the milk and all procedures for preservation of milk sample was taken by him.

In view of the testimony of P.W.-3, the court below did not find any infirmity in the procedure of obtaining sample and opined that the mandatory provisions of Rules 16 and 17 had been followed by the then Food Inspector.
Further, specific objection was taken by the accused regarding non compliance of the provisions of Section 13(2).
It was contended that the public analyst report was not provided within requisite period so as to get an independent analysis from the the Central Food Laboratory.
It is relevant to note that the trial court neither recorded any finding on the said issue nor noted anything about the compliance of mandatory provisions of Section 13(2) of the Act, 1954.

As per the public analyst report, milk fat was found deficient to the extent of 6.2%, whereas soluble non fat was deficient to the extent of 7.8%, as a result of which milk was found adulterated, i.e. it was opined water was added to the milk by the accused/revisionist.
A conclusion was, therefore, drawn that the revisionist is guilty of adulteration in violation of Section 7(1) of Act, 1954.
The appellate court upheld the conviction recording that the public analyst report was sent to the accused/revisionist through registered post Exhibit-Ka-9.

Noticing that there was sufficient compliance of the provisions of Section 13(2), it was held therein that there was no infirmity in the judgement of conviction as adulteration in milk was proved from the public analyst report.

Both the above decisions of the court below are under challenge in the present petition with the categorical submission by the learned counsel for the petitioner that there is clear violation of the Rules 16 & 17 of the Food Adulteration Rules, 1954.
The procedure for taking sample had not been followed by the Food Inspector.
Sanctioning authority did not apply its mind while granting sanction for lodging the prosecution against the revisionist.
The public analyst report was not served upon the revisionist within time and, as such, he did not get opportunity to verify the same by the Central Analysis Laboratory.
There is clear violation of Section 13(2) read with Rule 9B of the Prevention of Food and Adulteration Act, 1955.

entities.text: Prevention of Food and Adulteration Act, 1955
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text: Having gone through the judgements of the courts below, it is evident that there is no discussion in the order of conviction with regard to the service of public analyst report to the accused within time prescribed under Section 13(2) of the Food Adulteration Act.

The Apex Court in the case of Vijendra vs. State of UP reported in AIR 2019 SC 4351 has held that the requirement of Section 13(2) of the Food and Adulteration Act to send the report after institution of prosecution against the person within time prescribed under Rule 9B of Rules, 1955 is mandatory and substantial compliance of the said provision is needed to sustain the conviction.

sentences.text: A valuable right has been given to an accused to get an independent Analyst report by providing Rule 9B of the Rules, 1955 that Local (Health) Authority shall send the report based on which action is taken, within ten days after institution of the prosecution.
Sending such a report by registered post would not be substantial compliance of Section 13(2) of the Act, 1954.
The very purpose of furnishing such report is to enable the accused to seek for reference to the Central Food Laboratory for analysis, if he dissatisfied with the report.
Such safeguard provided to the accused under Section 13(2) of the Act, 1954 is valuable right.
In case, the report is send beyond the period prescribed under Rule 9B, the valuable right available to the accused to seek for independent analysis or reference stands defeated.
Since the accused is made to suffer penal consequences of prosecution, the provisions of Section 13(2) read with Rule 9(B) of Rules, 1955 have to be construed strictly.

In the light of the legal position noted above, in the instant case, it is found that the public analyst report was not sent nor it was proved that the said report was served on the accused/revisionist within 10 days of the lodging of the prosecution.
The revisionist, thus, did not get opportunity to analyse the sample through an independent analyst i.e. the Central Laboratory.

Further, it is also noteworthy that there was considerable delay in launching prosecution, in as much as, sample was taken on 29.12.1987 and after eight months of receipt of the public analyst report, sanction for prosecution was given and the complaint was filed on 28.09.1988.

Even if, it is accepted for a moment that the public analyst report was sent through registered post to the accused-revisionist was received by him, there was considerable delay in sending the same,
which has resulted in frustration of the right given to the accused-revisionist under Section 13(2) of the Act, 1954.
The reason being that it would not be possible to retain the same properties of milk for a period of approximately ten months.
The properties of the milk sample was bound to change during such a long period taken in launching prosecution and furnishing public analyst report to the revisionist.
It was, therefore, not possible for the accused/revisionist to get correct analysis of the milk sample.
From all angles, the conviction of the revisionist being in violation of the statutory provisions cannot be sustained.

The judgments and orders dated 30.7.1997 passed by the Additional Chief Judicial Magistrate,
Mainpuri and 10.3.1999 passed by the VI Additional Sessions Judge, Mainpuri; respectively, are hereby set aside.
The revisionist is acquitted of the charges under Section 7/16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.
The bail bonds furnished by the revisionist are discharged.
Fine, if paid, be refunded to the revisionist.
The revision is allowed.
